Stock vs mutual fund portfolios

Shares and open-end funds speak different measurement languages. Separate portfolios keep NAV tracking and FIFO share lots from colliding — while one account login still owns both books.

Why separate books

Equity portfolios care about share quantities, exchange marks and FIFO lots. Fund portfolios care about units and NAVs. Forcing both into one mash-up makes average cost and daily P&L harder to trust.

Separation is bookkeeping hygiene, not a marketing upsell.

Create and switch

Use the portfolio switcher to open a stock book or a mutual fund book. Each keeps its own holdings and history.

Name them clearly — for example “PSX shares” and “Open-end funds” — so imports land in the right place.

Sync and multi-device caution

Drive backup can cover the portfolios you use. After switching phones, confirm the portfolio name before editing.

Pending sync on portfolio A does not mean portfolio B is safe to overwrite casually. Finish one book’s sync story before juggling devices.

Practical workflow

Import broker equity trades into the stock portfolio. Enter fund statement lines into the fund portfolio. Review each on its own schedule.

When you reconcile, match each book to the right broker or AMC statement.

This guide is educational and describes how PSX Tracker works. It is not investment, tax or legal advice. Confirm rules and figures with your broker, FBR guidance and professional advisors.

Two books, one investor

Shares and fund units answer to different statements. The broker and CDC tell you about shares. The asset manager tells you about units. Putting both in one list feels tidy and makes every total harder to audit, because a “quantity” of 500 might be shares or units and a “price” might be a trade or a NAV.

PSX Tracker keeps a stock portfolio and a fund portfolio so the calculations stay in their own language. FIFO lots, board prices, and contract notes stay with the shares. Subscriptions, redemptions, and NAVs stay with the funds. A combined screen can add the market values afterward for a net-worth glance.

You can also keep more than one stock portfolio: a spouse’s holdings, a longer-term book, a smaller experimental book. Label them by the statement you will reconcile them to. “Growth” is a mood. “MCB account ending 1842” is a label you can check.

Cash is not a single pocket

Money at the broker is not money at the asset manager, and neither is money in your bank. The stock portfolio’s cash should explain the broker wallet: deposits, withdrawals, buys, sells, dividends, and fees. The fund portfolio should explain payments to and from the manager. Transferring a figure from one book to the other without an actual bank movement will make one side negative and the other magical.

A transfer of shares between two of your stock portfolios is not income and not a deposit. The shares leave one book at their cost and arrive in the other at that same cost. Recording the arrival at the market price creates a gain on a day you did not sell.

If you fund a fund subscription by withdrawing from the broker, record both events. The withdrawal is cash leaving the broker. The subscription is units arriving at the manager. Skipping either one makes net invested wrong, which makes every return percentage wrong.

Combined view without a combined mess

The useful combined number is market value plus the cash that belongs to you, across books. It is a snapshot. It is not a single FIFO stack and it is not a single tax figure. Taxes on a share sale and taxes on a fund redemption follow different statements. Add the values. Do not add the tax stories.

Performance against the KSE-100 should use the share book, or a combined book you understand, and should say which. An income fund will not track the index, and it should not be blamed for that in a chart labeled as equity performance.

Dividends from shares and distributions from funds can both be income and still should stay attached to the book that received them. Otherwise a later reconcile cannot tell which statement to open.

Day-to-day switching

Work in the book that matches the statement in front of you. If the broker PDF is open, you are in the stock portfolio. If the fund allocation email is open, you are in the fund portfolio. Switching first prevents the classic mistake of typing a fund subscription as a share buy of a made-up symbol.

The default broker on a stock portfolio is a convenience for new trades. It should be the broker on the statement. Trades from a second broker need the broker field changed, or they will reconcile to the wrong login.

Drive backup stores the set of portfolios, not one of them. A restore brings the set back. Check both books after a restore, not only the one you use daily. The quiet book is the one that gets stale.

When you should not merge

Do not merge a joint account into a personal one to see a bigger chart. Beneficial ownership matters for tax and for the argument you will have later. Keep the books apart and look at a combined view if you want the picture.

Do not merge history from before a corporate action with a fresh import that already includes the new shares, unless you have removed the overlap. Two sources for one fill is the most common double count.

If a merge is truly what you want, export both books, keep the files, and reconcile the result to both statements in the same sitting. A merge without that hour is how cash goes negative and stays there.

Common questions

Why are stocks and funds in different portfolios?

Shares use lot matching and a market price. Funds use units and NAV. Separate books keep those calculations from colliding.

Can I look at both together?

Yes. A combined view can sit on top of the separate books. The underlying records stay in their own portfolios.

What happens to Drive backup with several portfolios?

The snapshot saved to your Drive includes the portfolios in the app, not a second hidden book.
